title: Republicans play a numbers game in the House, and the number of the moment is 53
summary: Numbers are not kind to Republicans in the Maryland House, where Democrats hold a 102-39 advantage, but there's one number that was very good to the GOP this week: 53. That's the number of the House rule that let them twice stall bills for a day.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters January 31, 2026

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters January 31, 2026

Numbers are generally not kind to Republicans in Annapolis, where Democrats enjoy a 102-39 advantage in the House of Delegates and it’s difficult, if not impossible, for the GOP to have its way.

But there’s one number that’s been very good to House Republicans this week: 53.

That’s the number of the House rule that has been invoked twice by Republican members to stall progress on bills the House is debating, on proposals to restrict local participation in immigration enforcement and to redraw the state’s congressional district boundaries.

House Rule 53 allows any member, with the support of at least four others, to put a bill or an amendment on hold for one day if it is made in the first 65 days of the session; after day 65, the layover is an hour, and the motion can be challenged, unlike the first part of the session when a Rule 53 motion cannot be debated.

It was first invoked Thursday by Del. Matt Morgan (R-St. Mary’s) on an amendment he was proposing to the House redistricting bill, and was novel enough that Morgan had to remind colleagues that he needed at least four of them to stand in support of his motion.

It happened again Friday when Del. Robin Grammer Jr. (R-Baltimore County), after speaking for almost 8 minutes on a proposed amendment to a House bill that would prohibit 287(g) agreements between local police and federal immigration authorities, said that maybe the House needed “a little more investigation of this issue,” and asked to lay the bill over for a day. Grammer’s was the sixth amendment offered Friday to House Bill 444, one of two immigration enforcement bills sponsored by Del. Nicole Williams (D-Prince George’s).

Redistricting bill heads for final House vote as Democrats easily rebuff GOP amendments

After Grammer’s Rule 53 motion, House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel) conceded that “those are the rules,” then cautioned the minority about overuse of the rule when the House is already more than two weeks into a 90-day legislative session.

“I want to address the body for a minute,” Peña-Melnyk said. “I know it is the right of any one in this body to lay over a bill. It happened yesterday. It happened today. We have 74 days left in session, so I am going to ask you, respectfully, to use it judiciously …. We don’t want it to be overused.”

After Grammer laid over the immigration bill, the House returned to Morgan’s amendment of the day before on the redistricting bill and, after another 15 minutes of debate, rejected his amendment.

House Minority Leader Jason Buckel (R-Allegany) said laying over amendments on bills has some utility for a heavily outnumbered minority.

“We certainly, as a Republican Caucus, will typically special-order bills that we believe we have to present amendments on, and we did that both with the redistricting bill and the 287(g) bill,” Buckel said after the House adjourned. “Members have the right to utilize whatever rules they want to use, but we can’t then turn around and complain when other rules are invoked. So it works both ways.”

Del. C.T. Wilson (D-Charles), the sponsor of the congressional redistricting bill, who also serves as the House parliamentarian, said that Republicans have a “right to exercise” tactics like Rule 53. But he said it is also “the speaker’s right to reject at some point.”

“She’s trying to go forward in good faith,” Wilson said. “If it looks like it’s being dilatory, that’s a different story.”

Grammer’s motion Friday followed nearly 90 minutes of debate on HB 444 that was largely respectful, but with a bit of spice.

HB 444 is an emergency bill that would prohibit 287(g) agreements between local police agencies and Immigration and Customs Enforcement. In Maryland, the agreements are used for detainers: If local police have a suspect in another crime who they learn is undocumented, it can hold that person for 48 hours to hand over to ICE. Nine sheriff’s departments in the state currently have such agreeents and, as the bill is an emergency measure, those agreements would end immediately it the bill passed.

The spice started within the first few minutes of debate when House Minority Whip Jesse Pippy (R-Frederick) offered an amendment that would let local jurisdictions enter agreements “for the purpose of enforcing civil immigration law when an individual has been charged with committing a crime of violence.”

Williams, the bill’s sponsor, noted that individuals who were convicted of serious crimes wouldn’t be incarcerated in a local detention center, “they’re actually going to be in Jessup,” in the state prison.

A few minutes later, Pippy and House Majority Leader David Moon (D-Montgomery) disagreed on the meaning of Pippy’s amendment. Pippy asked Moon if he’s ever visited a jurisdiction with a 287(g) program.

“I have not visited a 287(g) program,” Moon said.

“How is it that the majority leader … has [not] taken the time to even visit the facility to understand what the program is?” Pippy asked.

“I don’t have to step into the facility to know that ICE is going to deport people before they do time in a Maryland facility under your amendment,” Moon said.

The House is scheduled to reconvene at 3 p.m. Monday, where the bill could receive preliminary approval. A Senate version of the bill could get final approval in that chamber on Tuesday.

While she conceded the right to lay over bills, and urged that it be used judiciously, Peña-Melnyk also reminded members that there are rules that benefit the speaker, too, if the maneuvering on the floor led to the House being backed up.

After Morgan’s motion Thursday, she told the House there “will not be a second layover of this bill,” and told delegates to come Friday with amendments in hand and ready to debate. On Friday, she put an edge on her statements.

“So, if we have to come on Saturdays and Sunday[s] to make sure that we do the work by the time we adjourn, I would like you to look at your calendars and make sure you clear your calendars because we may have to do that to move the work,” Peña-Melnyk said.

“This is respectfully stating it because it’s the second day we use it,” she said Friday. “I just want to make sure that we don’t overuse it because then we’re going to fall behind.”
